records.d: Max Mathews wrote the MUSIC program at Bell Labs in 1957, the first software for synthesizing sound on a computer. A machine could now produce organized sound from code. Personalized generated music starts here: music as computation.
records.h: MUSIC read a score of note instructions and computed audio waveforms sample by sample on an IBM 704, outputting to a digital-to-analog converter. Composers programmed sound instead of playing it. Music became data before it became personal.
records.mj: Established - documented 1957 Bell Labs program by Max Mathews.
records.t: 1957: MUSIC - the First Computer Music Program
records.z: timeline|year=1957|span=1|events=Max Mathews writes MUSIC at Bell Labs~first computer-synthesized sound

records.d: The Illiac Suite, composed in 1957 by Lejaren Hiller and Leonard Isaacson on the ILLIAC computer, was the first substantial music composed with a computer: algorithms generated the notes under composed rules. A machine participated in composition. The composer became a programmer of musical rules.
records.h: Markov chains and rule filters generated note sequences, with the composers selecting and refining the output into a string quartet score. The algorithm proposed; humans disposed. This propose-and-refine loop is still how AI music tools work.
records.mj: Established - documented 1957 composition by Hiller and Isaacson on ILLIAC.
records.t: 1957: the Illiac Suite - First Computer Composition

records.d: Sony's Walkman, launched in 1979, made music personal and portable: your soundtrack followed you through your day. Personalized music's oldest consumer form is the personal playlist, and the Walkman invented it. Generation would come later; personalization of listening came first.
records.h: A portable cassette player with lightweight headphones let individuals carry their chosen music anywhere. The mixtape became a personal art form. Private, mobile listening created the expectation that music follows the person, not the room.
records.mj: Established - documented 1979 Sony launch; portable personal listening.

records.d: The MIDI standard, finalized in 1983, let computers, synthesizers, and sequencers speak one control language. Generative algorithms could now drive any instrument. MIDI turned music into messages a program could compose in real time.
records.h: MIDI sent note-on, note-off, velocity, and control messages between devices at 31.25 kbaud, separating composition data from sound production. Any algorithm could output MIDI and hear itself. The protocol made generative music hardware-agnostic.
k: One control language for music devices
Music as messages programs can compose
records.mj: Established - MIDI 1.0 specification finalized 1983.

records.d: David Cope's Experiments in Musical Intelligence (EMI), developed through the 1980s, analyzed works of composers like Bach and composed convincing new pieces in their styles. A program passed as a dead master. Style itself proved computable.
records.h: EMI extracted signatures, patterns, and recombination rules from a composer's corpus, then generated new works following those rules. Experts struggled to distinguish EMI's Bach from Bach. Compositional style became an analyzable, reproducible model.
k: AI composing in the style of Bach
records.mj: Established - documented Cope EMI program; style-modeling composition in the 1980s.

records.d: LucasArts' iMUSE system, debuting in 1991, made game music adaptive: the score rearranged itself in real time as gameplay changed, with smooth transitions between musical states. Music began responding to the listener's situation. Adaptive music was born in adventure games.
records.h: iMUSE tracked game variables and triggered musical transitions, crossfades, and variations from a composed decision tree. The score was a state machine. Music that listens to context predates music that listens to taste.
records.mj: Established - documented 1991 LucasArts system; adaptive game music.
records.z: timeline|year=1991|span=1|events=iMUSE debuts in Monkey Island 2~adaptive game music begins

records.d: SSEYO's Koan, released in 1994, was consumer generative music software: users set rules and moods, and the program composed endless ambient pieces that never repeated. Brian Eno used it for generative installations. Endless personal music, on a home PC, in the nineties.
records.h: Koan's rule-based engine interpreted user-defined scales, probabilities, and voice behaviors to synthesize continuous MIDI music. Eno's 'Generative Music 1' shipped on floppy disk. The user was the composer of the rules; the PC was the performer.
records.mj: Established - documented 1994 SSEYO release; consumer generative music software.
records.z: formula|label=Koan endless minutes|a=24|b=60|op=mul|unit=minutes per day of music

records.d: Apple's iPod, launched in 2001 with '1,000 songs in your pocket,' made the personal music library portable at scale. Listeners carried their whole taste with them. The personal collection became data a machine could learn from.
records.h: A 5GB hard drive held a thousand MP3s with metadata: artist, genre, play counts, ratings. Listening became logged behavior. The library was the first dataset of personal musical taste.
records.mj: Established - documented 2001 Apple launch; portable personal music libraries.

records.d: Apple's iTunes Music Store, launched in April 2003, sold individual tracks digitally and tied purchases to personal accounts. Buying became a logged preference signal. The store learned what you liked because you told it with your wallet.
records.h: Account-linked purchases created per-user purchase histories, feeding recommendation experiments. The 99-cent single unbundled the album. Commerce generated the preference data that personalization runs on.
records.mj: Established - documented April 2003 launch; account-linked digital music retail.
records.t: 2003: iTunes Store - Buying as Taste Data

records.d: The Echo Nest, founded in 2005, built machine listening that analyzed millions of songs for tempo, mood, timbre, and structure: a robot musicologist. Spotify later bought it to power personalization. Taste became computable at catalog scale.
records.h: Audio-analysis models extracted acoustic features from recordings, building searchable similarity spaces across millions of tracks. Developers queried 'songs like this' by math. The catalog became a navigable space of sound.
k: Machine listening across millions of songs
records.mj: Established - documented 2005 founding; machine music analysis (later acquired by Spotify).

records.d: Spotify, launched in 2008, put tens of millions of songs behind a personal account with logged listening. The playlist became algorithmic and the library infinite. Personalization moved from owning songs to renting taste.
records.h: Streaming logged every play, skip, and save per user, feeding collaborative filtering and audio models. Access replaced ownership. The service knew your taste better than your record shelf did.
k: Tens of millions of songs, one account
records.mj: Established - documented 2008 launch; logged streaming listening at scale.

records.d: David Cope's Emily Howell program released the album 'From Darkness, Light' in 2009: composed by software, performed by humans. An AI had a discography. The composer-program graduated from experiment to recording artist.
records.h: Emily Howell extended EMI with associative networks, composing original works in its own developed style rather than imitating masters. Human musicians performed the scores. The program was credited as composer.
records.mj: Established - documented 2009 album release; Emily Howell credited as composer.
records.t: 2009: Emily Howell - the AI Recording Artist
records.z: timeline|year=2009|span=1|events=From Darkness, Light released~AI credited as composer

records.d: Spotify's Discover Weekly, launched in July 2015, gave every user a fresh personalized mixtape each Monday, built from listening behavior. Millions opened it weekly. Personalized curation became a habit, the mass-market proof that people want music chosen for them.
records.h: Collaborative filtering plus audio models assembled 30 tracks per user weekly from behavior patterns. The playlist felt hand-made. Curation, not generation, was the first personalization billions experienced.
records.mj: Established - documented July 2015 launch; personalized weekly playlists at scale.

c: Sony CSL Flow Machines records, September 2016
records.d: Sony's Flow Machines unveiled 'Daddy's Car' in September 2016: a pop song composed by AI in the style of the Beatles, arranged and produced by humans. The demo made AI songwriting headline news. Style transfer worked on the hit parade.
records.h: The system learned stylistic models from a corpus and generated lead sheets in the target style, which musician Benoît Carré arranged and produced. AI composed; humans produced. The collaboration model for AI hits was set.
records.mj: Established - documented September 2016 unveiling; Flow Machines Beatles-style composition.
records.t: 2016: Daddy's Car - AI Writes a Pop Song
records.z: timeline|year=2016|span=1|events=Daddy's Car unveiled~AI songwriting goes mainstream

records.d: Google's Magenta project released NSynth in April 2017: a neural synthesizer that learned the character of sounds and morphed between instruments, creating timbres no physical instrument could make. AI began inventing sounds, not just notes. The instrument itself became generative.
records.h: A variational autoencoder learned latent representations of instrument sounds; interpolating in latent space morphed a flute into a synth. New timbres were discovered, not designed. Sound design became latent-space exploration.
records.mj: Established - documented April 2017 Magenta release; neural audio synthesis.

records.d: Endel, which signed an AI-music deal with Warner Music in 2019, generated endless functional soundscapes adapting to time of day, weather, and heart rate: music for focus, sleep, and movement. Generative music found its first mass use case: wellness. The soundtrack began responding to the body.
records.h: Rule-based generative engines took contextual inputs, time, location, activity, and biosignals, and rendered adaptive ambient streams in real time. The 2019 Warner deal put AI-generated albums on streaming services. Function, not art, was the wedge.
k: Generative soundscapes for focus and sleep
Adapting to time, weather, heart rate
records.mj: Established - documented 2019 Warner Music deal; adaptive functional music.

records.d: OpenAI's MuseNet, announced in April 2019, generated four-minute compositions blending styles from Mozart to the Beatles on demand. A transformer learned composition across genres. Long-form, multi-style generation worked.
records.h: A transformer trained on MIDI files across styles generated coherent multi-instrument compositions from style and instrumentation prompts. Attention carried long-range structure. The model composed like it had studied everything.
records.mj: Established - documented April 2019 OpenAI release; transformer music generation.

records.d: OpenAI's Jukebox, announced in April 2020, generated raw audio, including rudimentary singing, in the style of specific artists from lyrics and genre prompts. AI sang. The voice joined the composition as a generative target.
records.h: VQ-VAE compression plus transformers modeled raw waveforms, generating stylized songs with vocals from text prompts. Quality was rough but the direction was clear. Audio, not just notes, became generatable.
records.mj: Established - documented April 2020 OpenAI release; raw-audio song generation.

records.d: By 2021, Boomy was letting anyone generate and release original songs in seconds, with users publishing millions of AI-assisted tracks to streaming services. Songwriting democratized to a button press. The barrier between listener and composer collapsed.
records.h: One-click generation pipelines composed, arranged, and mastered tracks from style choices, handling distribution to streaming platforms. Users curated rather than composed. Creation became selection.
records.mj: Established - documented platform growth; millions of user-generated tracks released.

records.d: Riffusion, released in December 2022, generated music by applying image diffusion to spectrograms: text prompts became sound. The prompt era reached music. Anyone could describe a song and hear it.
records.h: A Stable Diffusion model fine-tuned on spectrogram images generated new spectrograms from text, converted back to audio. Vision models made music. Text-to-music joined text-to-image as a consumer medium.
records.mj: Established - documented December 2022 release; text-to-music via spectrogram diffusion.
records.t: 2022: Riffusion - Describe a Song, Hear It

records.d: Spotify launched its AI DJ in February 2023: a synthetic host that built personalized sets with spoken commentary about your taste, in a generated voice. The radio DJ became personal software. Curation gained a voice that knew you.
records.h: Recommendation models selected tracks while a generative voice model delivered personalized commentary between songs. The host knew your history. Personal radio, hosted by software, for everyone.
records.mj: Established - documented February 2023 Spotify launch; personalized AI DJ.

records.d: Google's MusicLM, published in January 2023, generated high-fidelity music from rich text descriptions, handling prompts like 'a melancholic jazz trio at midnight.' Descriptive language became a compositional tool. The better you described the feeling, the better the song.
records.h: Hierarchical language modeling over audio tokens turned detailed captions into coherent multi-minute music. Text understanding drove musical decisions. Prompt craft became musicianship.
records.mj: Emerging - real published research (January 2023); text-to-music at high fidelity.

records.d: Suno, launched in December 2023, generated complete songs with vocals, lyrics, and arrangement from a single prompt, and went viral as millions made tracks. The song became a prompt output. Consumer songwriting hit the mainstream.
records.h: End-to-end models composed lyrics, melody, arrangement, and vocal synthesis from text prompts in under a minute. Sharing features spread creations socially. The loop from idea to finished song closed.
records.mj: Emerging - real launched product (December 2023); viral consumer song generation.

records.d: YouTube's Dream Track, announced in November 2023, let creators generate short songs in the licensed voices of participating artists from text prompts. Licensed synthetic voices entered the creator toolkit. The industry began licensing the future instead of fighting it.
records.h: Agreements with artists allowed voice models of their singing to generate new Shorts soundtracks from prompts. Consent was built in. Licensing, not litigation, became the industry's AI strategy.
records.mj: Emerging - real announced product (November 2023); licensed voice-model music generation.
records.z: timeline|year=2023|span=1|events=Dream Track announced~licensed synthetic artist voices

records.d: Udio, launched in April 2024, pushed consumer text-to-music quality further with emotive vocals and cleaner production, intensifying the song-generation race. Competition improved the art. The prompt-to-song pipeline became a product category.
records.h: Improved audio models generated more expressive vocals and mixes from prompts, with remix and extend features for iteration. Quality leapt in months. The category's pace mirrored the image-generation boom.
records.mj: Emerging - real launched product (April 2024); high-fidelity consumer song generation.

records.d: By 2024, adaptive music middleware was generating and rearranging scores in real time inside games and interactive film, responding to story state and player biometrics. The iMUSE idea, rebuilt with neural models. Scores breathed with the audience.
records.h: Real-time generation and stem-mixing engines took game-state and biometric inputs to compose adaptive scores on the fly. Music followed tension, not timelines. The film score's linearity began dissolving.
records.mj: Emerging - real middleware and productions; real-time adaptive generated scores.

records.d: By 2025, apps were piloting personalized generated soundtracks: workout apps composing to your pace, focus apps scoring your work sessions, games with endless personal scores. The background music of life became personal software. Every app its own composer.
records.h: Context APIs fed activity, time, and preference data to generative music engines rendering endless adaptive streams per user. The soundtrack followed the task. Music became infrastructure.
records.mj: Emerging - real pilots and products; personalized generated soundtracks in apps.

records.d: In this projected stage, music composes itself around your measured mood: biometric signals steer generative engines toward calm, energy, or focus in real time. The soundtrack reads you before you know how you feel. Your nervous system becomes the conductor.
records.h: Wearable biosignals would feed emotion-inference models driving generative music parameters: tempo, key, density, timbre. The loop would close in seconds. Music becomes biofeedback you can dance to.

records.d: In this projected stage, your music adapts second by second to what you are doing: cadence-matched running tracks, focus-deepening work scores, sleep-descending night music. The song never ends; it evolves with your activity. Life gets a continuous personal score.
records.h: Activity-recognition models would drive generative parameters continuously, crossfading musical material as tasks change. The stream would be endless and responsive. The album format dissolves into the lifelog.
records.mj: Signature-generated speculative projection — not established fact. No system adapts generated music second-by-second to activity today.

records.d: In this projected stage, a personal AI composer holds a lifelong model of your taste: every song you loved, skipped, or grew out of, informing compositions made only for you. It knows your phases. The composer of your life's soundtrack knows you better than any DJ could.
records.h: Long-term taste models would accumulate decades of listening signals, generating music that references your history and anticipates your evolution. The model would grow with you. Taste becomes a lifelong collaboration.
records.mj: Signature-generated speculative projection — not established fact. No AI holds a lifelong taste model composing for one person today.

records.d: In this projected stage, shared spaces get shared adaptive music: a dinner party's soundtrack blending everyone's taste, a gym floor's energy negotiated across members. Personal music becomes social. The DJ is an algorithm with everyone's preferences.
records.h: Multi-user preference models would negotiate a musical compromise in real time, weighting tastes and reading the room's response. The mix would be a social computation. Background music becomes groupware.
records.mj: Signature-generated speculative projection — not established fact. No system negotiates shared adaptive music across a group today.

records.d: In this projected stage, concerts remix themselves per listener: the same live show rendered with personalized mixes, alternate arrangements, and AR overlays tuned to each attendee. Ten thousand people, ten thousand versions of the night. The gig becomes personal.
records.h: Object-based live audio plus generative arrangement would let each listener's device remix the performance feed in real time. The artist performs once; software performs ten thousand times. Liveness and personalization merge.
records.mj: Signature-generated speculative projection — not established fact. No concert remixes itself per listener today.

records.d: In this projected stage, music is generated from your memories and dreams: sleep data and lifelogs becoming compositions that sound like your past felt. The most personal music of all. Your life, scored from the inside.
records.h: Memory and dream-report models would map autobiographical material to musical parameters: places to timbres, eras to styles, emotions to harmony. The composition would be an autobiography in sound. Nostalgia becomes an instrument.
k: Places mapped to timbres, eras to styles
records.mj: Signature-generated speculative projection — not established fact. No system composes from memories and dreams today.

records.d: In this projected stage, the living personal soundtrack is the working version: music that has followed you all day, adapting to every task and mood, composed by an AI that knows your whole taste history. You never press play; the music is simply there, always right. The jukebox finally disappears into life.
records.h: Always-on generative engines with full context awareness would render a continuous personal score across devices, anticipating needs from calendar, biometrics, and habit. Playback becomes ambience. The interface vanishes; the music remains.
records.mj: Signature-generated speculative projection — not established fact. No always-on living personal soundtrack exists today.
